implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: keep the versions of the attribute in an ordered store keyed by their effective start (a 'temporal collection' with get(time point) / put(time point, value) and a milestones traversal), and expose the owning object's property twice - an accessor parameterised by a Time Point, which answers 'what was the value on 2 Feb 1998?', and a no-argument accessor that asks the same question about a default time point, normally today. Model additive updates as put(value, effective-from), where a past date is a retroactive correction, today's is a current change and a future date is a scheduled change; model insertion updates as a reference to the version covering an existing range plus a new range, because the same value can be valid in two disjoint intervals. When the store is relational, the collection does not map naively: it becomes Effectivity on the value (or an intersection table with from/to columns), and the accessor is what keeps that mapping out of the rest of the model. Keep stored versions immutable and the store append-only; add a second (recorded/transaction) time dimension only when corrections themselves must be reconstructable.
code_sketch:
# owning object
salaryAt(date)        -> value of the version in force on `date`
salary()              -> salaryAt(today())            # default time point
setSalary(amount, from) -> collection.put(from, amount)  # back-dating allowed

# temporal collection: milestones keyed by effective start date
collection.get(1998-02-02) -> walk back from the newest start <= date -> 154 Norwood Rd
collection.put(1998-08-23, "15 Damon Ave")   # additive update, effective from that date
collection.milestones()   -> [1998-08-23, 1998-01-01, 1985-09-01]  # newest first
pitfalls: Letting callers see the effectivity rows or the milestone list recreates the coupling the pattern removes.
Storing mutable value objects in the collection: a later in-place edit rewrites history without leaving a version.
An implicit 'today' in the no-argument accessor applied inside domain logic, which makes results depend on the clock.
Unbounded, unpruned history with no retention policy, presented as compliance.

Wrong move: let writers and readers disagree about whether the effective-from date belongs to the old or the new version; failure: a read on the exact changeover date returns the wrong value and adjacent ranges overlap or leave a one-day gap; instead: state one half-open [from, to) convention in the collection and test the exact switchover instant (vendor as-of syntax even splits into FROM..TO and BETWEEN..AND forms because this boundary is contested).

Wrong move: query the raw history table as an authoritative audit of every intermediate value; failure: several changes in one transaction land as zero-duration versions (or vanish when period timestamps lack precision) and direct reads expose states that were never committed; instead: read history only through the as-of accessor, keep full period precision, and use real auditing when intermediate states must be recorded.
